lead: Xen, VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V are Type 1 hypervisors. Each runs directly on the physical host and shares it among virtual machines. They differ in how they manage devices. Xen uses a privileged control domain called Dom0. VMware ESXi uses its own VMkernel. Hyper-V uses a privileged parent or root partition. These management domains are not ordinary guest workloads. The examples show real control-domain designs, not just product names. Use them to answer exam questions on hypervisor architecture and on the path a device request takes.
prereq: You need 3.3 for the hypervisor role and 3.4 for full and para-virtualization, including hypercalls.

sections.h3: Xen: Dom0, DomU, PV and HVM

blocks.text: Xen puts a small hypervisor directly on the hardware. The hypervisor schedules vCPUs, controls memory and delivers interrupts, but it does not hold full disk and network drivers. That work sits in a special virtual machine.

Dom0 is the first domain and the privileged control domain. It runs a full OS, device drivers and the toolstack that creates, starts and stops guests. DomU is an unprivileged guest domain. A DomU cannot read Dom0 memory or another DomU memory; the hypervisor enforces that boundary.

Xen guests run in two modes. A paravirtualized (PV) guest has a modified OS and uses hypercalls for privileged operations. An HVM (hardware virtual machine) guest is unmodified and uses hardware virtualization from Intel VT-x or AMD-V; QEMU, a device emulator in Dom0, emulates some devices for it. PV drivers can be added to an HVM guest to speed up disk and network I/O.

Device path in Xen: a DomU writes to a shared memory ring, a Dom0 backend driver reads it, and the Dom0 driver talks to the physical device. Dom0 is therefore both a control domain and often a driver domain. It consumes host CPU and RAM like any VM, but its privilege is much higher.

VMware ESXi is a Type 1 hypervisor that runs on bare metal. Its core is the VMkernel. The VMkernel schedules vCPUs, manages memory, runs the storage stack, runs the network stack and loads physical device drivers. ESXi has no general-purpose service console; management comes from outside.

vSphere is the management suite around ESXi. vCenter Server is the central manager for many ESXi hosts. A vSphere Client or API talks to vCenter or to a single host. vSphere is not the hypervisor; ESXi is. This is a common exam confusion.

Device path in ESXi: a guest writes to a virtual NIC or virtual disk. The VMkernel receives that request, applies its virtual switch or storage rules, and calls the physical driver. The guest never programs the physical device directly. Isolation is enforced by the VMkernel, which keeps each VM's memory and virtual devices separate.
ESXi stores VM files on VMFS, a clustered file system, or on NFS. Live migration of a running VM is vMotion. These are management and storage features, not the definition of a Type 1 hypervisor.

Microsoft Hyper-V is a Type 1 hypervisor, but it is installed with a Windows parent partition. The hypervisor runs beneath that partition. The parent partition, also called the root partition in newer documentation, runs Windows and the virtualization stack. It owns most physical devices and creates child partitions.

A child partition holds a guest OS. It has no direct hardware access. Hyper-V provides synthetic devices through VMBus, an in-memory channel between parent and child. The parent has a virtual service provider (VSP); the child has a virtual service client (VSC). A request goes child VSC → VMBus → parent VSP → parent driver → hardware. Emulated devices exist for boot, but they are slower.

Hyper-V is called a microkernel design because the hypervisor is small and drivers stay in the parent. Isolation is still enforced by the hypervisor: child partitions cannot access each other's memory or the parent's memory. The parent is privileged, not an ordinary guest.

blocks.text: All three isolate guest memory; the hypervisor enforces the boundary. The difference is where drivers and management live: a separate Dom0, the VMkernel itself, or the Hyper-V parent partition. Some syllabi call these three case studies.

figure.caption: Dom0 is the privileged control domain, but its 2 vCPU and 4 GB still count. With six DomU guests, the host allocates 26 vCPU and 52 GB, leaving 6 cores and 76 GB free.

spec.title: Xen host: 32 cores, 128 GB
spec.aria: A block diagram of a Xen host with 32 cores and 128 GB RAM: Dom0 uses 2 vCPU and 4 GB, six DomU use 24 vCPU and 48 GB, total allocated is 26 vCPU and 52 GB, and free is 6 cores and 76 GB.

examples.question: A Xen host has 32 CPU cores and 128 GB RAM. Dom0 is given 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM. Six DomU guests are created, each with 4 vCPU and 8 GB RAM. Assume one vCPU maps to one physical core and no overcommit. (a) Find total vCPU allocated and cores still free. (b) Find total RAM allocated and RAM still free.
steps: Total vCPU allocated = Dom0 2 + DomU 24 = 26 vCPU.
Total RAM allocated = Dom0 4 GB + DomU 48 GB = 52 GB.
examples.answer: 26 vCPU are allocated and 6 cores remain free; 52 GB RAM is allocated and 76 GB RAM remains free.
examples.check:
cores = 32
ram = 128
dom0_vcpu = 2
dom0_ram = 4
guests = 6
guest_vcpu = 4
guest_ram = 8
total_vcpu = dom0_vcpu + guests * guest_vcpu
free_cores = cores - total_vcpu
total_ram = dom0_ram + guests * guest_ram
free_ram = ram - total_ram
print(total_vcpu)
print(free_cores)
print(total_ram)
print(free_ram)

traps: Dom0 in Xen and the parent partition in Hyper-V are privileged management domains. They are not ordinary guest workloads, and their CPU and RAM count in host allocation.
ESXi is the Type 1 hypervisor. vSphere and vCenter Server are management products. Do not call vSphere the hypervisor in an exam answer.
Xen HVM does not mean no PV drivers. An HVM guest can use PV drivers for faster disk and network I/O; QEMU is mainly for emulated devices and boot.
VMBus is an in-memory communication channel, not a physical bus. A child partition reaches hardware through a parent VSP and a parent driver.
All three isolate guest memory, but they place drivers differently: Dom0, VMkernel, or parent partition. The placement changes the device path, not the need for isolation.

quiz.a: Dom0 is the privileged control domain. It runs drivers and the toolstack, and it creates and manages DomU guests.

quiz.q: What is the VMkernel in VMware ESXi?
quiz.a: The VMkernel is the ESXi hypervisor core. It schedules vCPUs, manages memory, runs storage and network stacks, and loads physical device drivers.

quiz.q: Why does Xen keep physical device drivers in Dom0 instead of the hypervisor?
quiz.a: It keeps the hypervisor small and reduces the privileged code in the hypervisor. Drivers run in a separate privileged VM, while the hypervisor still enforces memory and CPU isolation.

quiz.q: Why is Hyper-V called a microkernel hypervisor even though Windows runs in the parent partition?
quiz.a: The hypervisor layer itself is small and does not contain most drivers. Drivers and management run in the parent partition, which sits under the hypervisor's control.

quiz.q: A Hyper-V host has 16 CPU cores and 64 GB RAM. The parent partition uses 2 vCPU and 4 GB. Four child partitions each use 2 vCPU and 6 GB. Find total vCPU allocated, free cores, total RAM allocated and free RAM. Assume one vCPU maps to one core and no overcommit.
quiz.a: Child vCPU = 4 × 2 = 8. Total vCPU = 2 + 8 = 10, so free cores = 16 − 10 = 6. Child RAM = 4 × 6 GB = 24 GB. Total RAM = 4 + 24 = 28 GB, so free RAM = 64 − 28 = 36 GB.

quiz.q: Compare the device path of a Xen DomU and a Hyper-V child partition. Name the analogous components.
quiz.a: Xen: DomU → shared ring → Dom0 backend driver → physical driver. Hyper-V: child VSC → VMBus → parent VSP → parent driver. The Dom0 backend driver is analogous to the parent VSP; the shared ring and VMBus are both communication channels; Dom0 is analogous to the parent partition.

quiz.q: A student says ESXi is Type 2 because vCenter manages it. Correct the statement.
quiz.a: The type depends on where the hypervisor runs, not on where management runs. ESXi runs directly on bare metal, so it is Type 1. vCenter is an external management layer and does not make ESXi Type 2.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, Xen appears in open-source cloud stacks, ESXi in private-cloud estates, and Hyper-V in Windows-centred data centres. Newer designs often split the control plane from the data plane, much like Dom0 and the Hyper-V parent. Search for “Xen driver domain”, “Hyper-V VMBus synthetic device” and “ESXi VMkernel” to go deeper.
